<reason>This was a tightly matched debate, but CON (A) built a more concrete and consistently safety-grounded case (dosing checks, allergy alerts, "2 a.m. accountability") that PRO's conformance-testing and stable-interface answers addressed only abstractly. PRO's best moment was its closing catch that CON's fallback to "rebid at renewal" leverage is hollow without actual portability — a genuinely sharp structural point. But because CON's closing came last chronologically, CON got to answer it directly (vendors can and do lose entire contracts at renewal even without mandated data portability), partially defusing the point rather than leaving it live. Both sides handled pressure questions with proper A1/A2 structure and real engagement, but CON's rebuttals (optional-field standards friction, module interdependency, poor-district capacity) landed with slightly more vivid, domain-specific force, and CON's closing framing ("leverage you can file vs. safety you can use") was more memorable. PRO's opening being clipped for length is a minor but real execution cost. Overall CON edges the debate on rebuttal resolution and rhetorical clarity, though PRO's leverage/lock-in case remained a credible, well-argued route throughout.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing move exposing that CON's "rebid at renewal" leverage claim contradicts CON's own admission that switching costs are dominated by retraining, forcing CON to defend that rebids are credible even without portability — CON's last-word rebuttal (vendors do execute full migrations at renewal) narrowly held the line but didn't fully dissolve the tension.</best_rebuttal>
